theorems.name: Irrationality of √2
theorems.statement: The square root of 2 is not a rational number (√2 ∉ ℚ)
hypotheses: √2 is expressible as p/q where p, q ∈ ℤ, q ≠ 0, and gcd(p, q) = 1 (fraction in lowest terms)
theorems.conclusion: The hypothesis leads to a logical contradiction; therefore no such representation exists and √2 ∉ ℚ

theorems.name: Parity Lemma (auxiliary)
theorems.statement: For any integer n, if n² is even then n is even
theorems.conclusion: n² even ⟹ n even (equivalently, by contrapositive: n odd ⟹ n² odd)

steps: Step 1 — Assume for contradiction: √2 = p/q with p, q ∈ ℤ, q ≠ 0, gcd(p, q) = 1 (lowest-terms representation exists by the well-ordering of ℤ)
Step 2 — Square both sides: (√2)² = (p/q)² ⟹ 2 = p²/q² ⟹ p² = 2q²
Step 3 — Parity cascade (part A): p² = 2q² means p² is even. By the Parity Lemma, p must be even. Write p = 2k for some k ∈ ℤ.
Step 4 — Substitute p = 2k into p² = 2q²: (2k)² = 2q² ⟹ 4k² = 2q² ⟹ q² = 2k²
Step 5 — Parity cascade (part B): q² = 2k² means q² is even. By the Parity Lemma, q must be even.
Step 6 — Contradiction: both p and q are even, so 2 | gcd(p, q). This contradicts the hypothesis that gcd(p, q) = 1.
Step 7 — Conclusion: The assumption that √2 ∈ ℚ is false; therefore √2 ∉ ℚ.

premises: ∀n ∈ ℤ: n² even ⟹ n even  (Parity Lemma)
Every rational number has a unique representation p/q with gcd(p, q) = 1
rules: Reductio ad absurdum: assume P, derive ⊥, conclude ¬P
Divisibility: 2 | p and 2 | q ⟹ 2 | gcd(p, q)

gaps.description: The Parity Lemma itself (n² even ⟹ n even) is invoked but not proved inline. A complete proof requires its justification.
gaps.suggestedFix: Prove by contrapositive: assume n is odd, so n = 2m + 1. Then n² = 4m² + 4m + 1 = 2(2m² + 2m) + 1, which is odd. Therefore n² odd ⟺ n odd, equivalently n² even ⟺ n even.

implicitAssumptions.statement: Every non-zero rational number can be written in lowest terms p/q with gcd(p, q) = 1
implicitAssumptions.suggestedFormulation: By the Well-Ordering Principle applied to |q| > 0, every rational has a least-denominator representation; dividing numerator and denominator by their GCD yields the lowest-terms form.

implicitAssumptions.statement: The integers ℤ are closed under multiplication and the notion of 'even' (divisible by 2) is well-defined
implicitAssumptions.suggestedFormulation: Standard property of ℤ under ring axioms; no further elaboration needed at this level.

unjustifiedSteps: Parity Lemma used without proof at Step 3 and Step 5 — minor gap addressable by the contrapositive sub-proof noted above
suggestions: State the Parity Lemma as an explicit sub-theorem before the main proof
For full formality, cite the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (prime factorization) as an alternative basis: 2 | p² ⟹ 2 | p because 2 is prime

dependencies: Definition of rational number (ℚ = { p/q | p, q ∈ ℤ, q ≠ 0 })
Parity Lemma: n² even ⟹ n even (provable by contrapositive)
Well-Ordering Principle of ℤ (guarantees lowest-terms representation exists)
Definition of gcd and the property gcd(p, q) = 1 ⟹ p and q share no common factor > 1
Divisibility: a | b and a | c ⟹ a | gcd(b, c)
assumptions: gcd is well-defined for all pairs of non-zero integers
2 is a prime integer (used to justify the Parity Lemma via Euclid's Lemma as an alternative)
references: Euclid, Elements Book X (attributed c. 300 BCE) — earliest recorded proof of irrationality
